content: Emergency medicine is a specialized branch of medicine practiced in hospital emergency departments, in the field by emergency medical services such as paramedics, and in other locations where initial medical treatment for acute illnesses or injuries is provided. Emergency physicians and allied healthcare workers in emergency departments operate under a triage system, prioritizing care based on the severity of a patient’s condition. The primary focus of emergency medicine is the diagnosis and treatment of acute illnesses and injuries that require immediate medical attention. While emergency medicine does not typically involve long-term or continuous care, emergency physicians and paramedics aim to improve long-term patient outcomes through their interventions. Urgent care centers, often staffed by physicians, nurses, and nurse practitioners, provide primary care for patients requiring immediate attention but whose conditions do not meet the acuity level necessitating emergency department care. These providers may or may not have formal training in emergency medicine. Emergency medicine encompasses a broad spectrum of general medicine and integrates knowledge and skills from nearly all medical specialties, including surgical sub-specialties. Emergency physicians are responsible for managing a high volume of patients, treating their conditions, and determining their disposition—whether admission to the hospital or discharge after treatment. Emergency physicians require extensive knowledge and advanced procedural skills, including surgical techniques, trauma resuscitation, advanced cardiac life support, and airway management. They are expected to possess the expertise of multiple specialists, such as managing complex airways (anesthesia), suturing intricate lacerations (plastic surgery), reducing fractures or dislocations (orthopedic surgery), treating myocardial infarctions (internal medicine), evaluating obstetric emergencies (obstetrics and gynecology), and controlling severe epistaxis (ENT). The International Federation for Emergency Medicine defines emergency medicine as a medical specialty focused on the prevention, diagnosis, and management of acute and urgent aspects of illness and injury across all age groups. It also involves understanding the development of pre-hospital and in-hospital emergency medical systems and the skills required for their implementation. Historically, the concept of emergency medicine can be traced back to the French Revolution, when Dominique Jean Larrey, a French military surgeon, introduced the idea of flying ambulances to rapidly transport wounded soldiers to centralized field hospitals. Larrey’s innovations laid the groundwork for modern emergency medical systems, and he is often regarded as the father of emergency medicine. As a formal medical specialty, emergency medicine is relatively young. Before the 1960s and 1970s, hospital emergency rooms were staffed by rotating physicians from various specialties, including general surgery, internal medicine, psychiatry, and dermatology. The chaotic nature of emergency departments during this period led to the establishment of emergency medicine as a distinct specialty. Groups of physicians began dedicating their practice exclusively to emergency care, with the first such group led by Dr. James DeWitt Mills at Alexandria Hospital, Virginia, in 1961. This initiative, known as the Alexandria Plan, provided 24/7 emergency care and marked the beginning of emergency medicine as a dedicated field. In 1979, emergency medicine was officially recognized as a medical specialty following the establishment of the American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) and the development of emergency medicine training programs. The American Board of Medical Specialties subsequently approved emergency medicine as a recognized specialty. Globally, various organizations oversee emergency medicine training and certification. In the United States, ACEP is the largest member organization for emergency physicians, with membership open to both allopathic (MD, MBBS) and osteopathic (DO) physicians. The American College of Osteopathic Emergency Physicians (ACOEP) and the American Academy of Emergency Medicine (AAEM) also play significant roles in the field. Certification is provided by bodies such as the American Board of Emergency Medicine (ABEM) and the American Osteopathic Board of Emergency Medicine (AOBEM). In the United Kingdom and Ireland, the College of Emergency Medicine oversees training and examinations for emergency physicians. In Australia and New Zealand, the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine (ACEM) manages advanced training in the specialty. In Canada, emergency medicine training follows two pathways: a five-year specialist residency certified by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada or a family medicine residency with an additional year of emergency medicine training through the College of Family Physicians of Canada (CCFP-EM). Emergency physicians are trained to handle a wide range of medical, surgical, and psychiatric emergencies. They are considered specialists in stabilizing and treating emergent conditions, making them both clinical generalists and skilled diagnosticians. Fellowship opportunities in emergency medicine include subspecialties such as toxicology, sports medicine, ultrasound, and pediatric emergency medicine. Emergency physicians typically work in hospital emergency departments on a shift basis, reflecting the 24/7 nature of emergency care. Employment arrangements vary and may include private practice, institutional contracts, corporate staffing, or governmental employment. The Advanced Medical Priority Dispatch System (AMPDS) is a software tool used by ambulance services worldwide to prioritize emergency calls. It categorizes calls into response levels—A (immediately life-threatening), B (urgent), and C (routine)—and assigns subcategories for statistical and performance analysis. This system helps improve response times and refine call triage processes.
